demoniac-in-synagogue-luk.quote: Jesus rebuked him, saying, “Be silent and come out of him!” When the demon had thrown him down in the middle of them, he came out of him, having done him no harm.
details: It happened in the synagogue, in front of the congregation.
Luke adds that the man was left unharmed.
The crowd's question was about authority and power, not about the man.
demoniac-in-synagogue-luk.whatHappened: In the synagogue at Capernaum a man cried out with a loud voice, naming Jesus correctly. Jesus told the spirit to be silent and come out. It threw the man down in front of everyone and left him — and Luke adds that it did him no harm.
demoniac-in-synagogue-luk.hopeMeaning: Luke pauses to tell you the man was not injured. That is a small clause and an easy one to skip, and it is the difference between a display of power and someone being looked after.
demoniac-in-synagogue-luk.reflectionQuestion: When something is finally dealt with, do you expect to come through it damaged?
demoniac-in-synagogue-luk.distinctive: Luke alone notes that the spirit did the man no harm as it left. Mark's version, which opens his whole Gospel, ends on the crowd's astonishment at the authority. Luke keeps the astonishment but adds the medical detail, which is his habit throughout: he tells you how the person was afterwards.

peters-mother-in-law-luk.quote: He stood over her and rebuked the fever, and it left her. Immediately she rose up and served them.
details: Luke calls it a great fever — he grades the severity.
Jesus rebuked the fever, the same verb used for driving out spirits.
She was up and serving immediately.
peters-mother-in-law-luk.whatHappened: They asked Jesus about Peter's wife's mother, who was down with a high fever. He stood over her and rebuked the fever as though speaking to it. It left her, and she got up at once and waited on them.
peters-mother-in-law-luk.hopeMeaning: The illness is addressed directly, spoken to rather than merely removed. Whatever else that means, it treats the thing making her ill as something with no right to be there.
peters-mother-in-law-luk.reflectionQuestion: What have you been enduring that might be worth confronting instead?
peters-mother-in-law-luk.distinctive: Luke alone grades it as a great fever, and alone has Jesus stand over her and rebuke it — the verb he uses for confronting unclean spirits. Matthew has a touch of the hand; Mark has Him take her hand and raise her up. Luke's is the only version where the fever is treated as an adversary.

catch-of-fish-luk.quote: Simon answered him, “Master, we worked all night and caught nothing; but at your word I will let down the net.”
details: They were professional fishermen being told how to fish by a carpenter's son.
They had already worked all night and caught nothing.
The catch was so large that two boats began to sink.
catch-of-fish-luk.whatHappened: After a night of catching nothing, Simon was told to put out into deep water and let down the nets. He said plainly that they had worked all night for nothing — and did it anyway. The catch nearly broke the nets and began sinking two boats. Simon fell down and asked Jesus to leave, calling himself a sinful man.
catch-of-fish-luk.hopeMeaning: His response to abundance is not delight but panic — he asks Jesus to go away. Being given far more than you asked for can be frightening rather than reassuring, and Luke lets that stand without correcting it.
catch-of-fish-luk.reflectionQuestion: Has something good ever arrived and made you want to back away from it?

leper-cleansed-luk.quote: He stretched out His hand and touched him, saying, “I want to. Be made clean.” Immediately the leprosy left him.
details: Luke describes him as a man full of leprosy — the disease was advanced.
He fell on his face rather than kneeling.
Afterwards Jesus withdrew into the desert and prayed.
leper-cleansed-luk.whatHappened: A man far gone with leprosy fell on his face and said that Jesus could make him clean if He were willing. Jesus touched him and said He was willing, and it left him at once. As the reports spread and crowds gathered, Jesus withdrew into the desert to pray.
leper-cleansed-luk.hopeMeaning: The account ends not with the crowds but with Jesus going away alone to pray. Luke keeps putting that in — the withdrawal after the work, as though it were part of the work.
leper-cleansed-luk.reflectionQuestion: What do you do immediately after something goes well?
leper-cleansed-luk.distinctive: Luke alone says the man was full of leprosy, and alone ends the scene with Jesus withdrawing into the desert to pray while the crowds grow. Mark ends with the healed man's talking making towns impossible to enter; Matthew ends at the priest. Luke turns the camera to what Jesus did next, on His own.

paralytic-luk.quote: Not finding a way to bring Him in because of the multitude, they went up to the housetop and let Him down through the tiles with His cot into the middle before Jesus.
details: Luke has them remove tiles, where Mark has them dig through.
Luke notes the Pharisees and teachers had come from every village of Galilee, Judea and Jerusalem.
The crowd's verdict: we have seen strange things today.
paralytic-luk.whatHappened: The house was so full — Luke says teachers had come from everywhere — that the men carrying a paralysed friend could not get in. They went up on the roof, removed tiles, and lowered him into the middle of the room. Jesus spoke about forgiveness first, then told him to get up. He went home glorifying God, and the crowd said they had seen strange things that day.
paralytic-luk.hopeMeaning: The room was full of experts, and the man got in through the ceiling. Luke's crowd does not conclude anything doctrinal; they just say they have seen something strange. Sometimes that is the honest first response.
paralytic-luk.reflectionQuestion: Is there something you have witnessed that you have never quite explained to yourself?
paralytic-luk.distinctive: Luke has tiles where Mark has them dig through the roof, and Matthew has no roof at all. Luke alone lists where the watching Pharisees and teachers had travelled from, and alone ends with the crowd's line — we have seen strange things today — rather than with praise for authority given to men.

withered-hand-luk.quote: He said to the man who had the withered hand, “Rise up and stand in the middle.” He arose and stood.
details: Luke specifies it was his right hand — the working hand.
Jesus made him stand up in the middle of the room before anything happened.
The watchers were left filled with rage.
withered-hand-luk.whatHappened: In the synagogue, watched by people looking for a charge, Jesus told a man with a withered right hand to get up and stand where everyone could see. Then He asked whether the Sabbath was for doing good or harm. He told the man to stretch out his hand, and it was restored — and the watchers were filled with rage.
withered-hand-luk.hopeMeaning: The man was made to stand in the middle first, exposed, before anything was fixed. Being seen came before being healed, which is harder and, in this account, deliberate.
withered-hand-luk.reflectionQuestion: Would you be willing to be visible about something before it is resolved?
withered-hand-luk.distinctive: Luke alone specifies the right hand — the one a man works with — and alone has Jesus make him stand in the middle of the room first. Mark records Jesus' anger and grief; Matthew argues from the sheep in the pit. Luke stages it, putting the man in full view before the question is even asked.

centurions-servant-luk.quote: For I also am a man placed under authority, having under myself soldiers. I tell this one, ‘Go!’ and he goes; and to another, ‘Come!’ and he comes; and to my servant, ‘Do this,’ and he does it.
details: The centurion never meets Jesus in Luke's account — he sends others.
Jewish elders argued his case: he loves our nation and built our synagogue.
He sent friends to stop Jesus before He reached the house.
centurions-servant-luk.whatHappened: A centurion's servant was dying. He sent Jewish elders to ask on his behalf, and they argued that he deserved the help because he had built their synagogue. As Jesus approached the house, the man sent friends out to say he was not worthy to have Him come under his roof — a word would do. The servant was found well.
centurions-servant-luk.hopeMeaning: Two things are said about the same man in the same story: he is worthy, say the elders; I am not worthy, says he. Luke lets both stand, and the healing happens regardless of which is true.
centurions-servant-luk.reflectionQuestion: Whose assessment of you do you tend to believe — other people's, or your own?
centurions-servant-luk.distinctive: Luke gives the whole story at one remove. The centurion never appears in person: elders come first with an argument for his worthiness, then friends with his denial of it. Matthew has him walk up and speak for himself. Luke's version is the one about how a community speaks for someone who will not speak for himself.

widows-son-at-nain-luk.quote: When the Lord saw her, He had compassion on her and said to her, “Don’t cry.”
details: He was her only son, and she was already a widow — she had no one left.
Nobody asked Jesus to do anything; He was simply passing the gate.
He touched the coffin, which made Him ritually unclean.
widows-son-at-nain-luk.whatHappened: Arriving at the town gate of Nain, Jesus met a funeral coming out: a widow's only son, with a crowd from the town. Nobody asked Him for anything. He saw her, told her not to cry, touched the coffin so the bearers stopped, and told the young man to get up. He sat up and began to speak, and Jesus gave him back to his mother.
widows-son-at-nain-luk.hopeMeaning: There is no request, no faith mentioned, and no conversation — only a woman who had lost everything, met by someone going the other way. The account's last clause is the point: He gave him to his mother.
widows-son-at-nain-luk.reflectionQuestion: Could you accept help you had not asked for and had not earned?

calming-storm-luk.quote: He awoke and rebuked the wind and the raging of the water; then they ceased, and it was calm.
details: Luke says the boat was filling and they were in real danger.
They call Him Master, twice over, rather than accusing Him.
His question afterwards is simply: where is your faith?
calming-storm-luk.whatHappened: A squall came down on the lake while Jesus slept, and the boat began to fill. The disciples woke Him crying Master, Master, we are dying. He rebuked the wind and the water, and it went calm. Then He asked where their faith was, and they asked each other who this could be.
calming-storm-luk.hopeMeaning: The question is not why they had no faith but where it had gone — as though it were somewhere, mislaid rather than absent. That is a gentler diagnosis than it first sounds.
calming-storm-luk.reflectionQuestion: If your faith is not absent but mislaid, where did you last have it?
calming-storm-luk.distinctive: Luke's disciples say "Master, Master" — respectful, not accusing, where Mark has them ask whether He cares that they are dying. And Luke's question afterwards is "Where is your faith?" rather than Matthew's "O you of little faith" or Mark's "how is it that you have no faith?" Luke assumes it exists and has been misplaced.

gerasene-demoniac-luk.quote: They came to Jesus and found the man from whom the demons had gone out, sitting at Jesus’ feet, clothed and in his right mind; and they were afraid.
details: Luke says he had gone without clothes and lived in the tombs for a long time.
Afterwards he is found sitting at Jesus' feet — the posture of a student.
He begged to come along and was sent home instead.
gerasene-demoniac-luk.whatHappened: A man who had lived naked among the tombs for years met Jesus on the shore. What held him was sent into a herd of pigs, which drowned. The townspeople came out and found him sitting at Jesus' feet, dressed and in his right mind — and they were frightened and asked Jesus to leave. The man begged to go with Him and was told to go home and tell what God had done.
gerasene-demoniac-luk.hopeMeaning: He wanted to leave with Jesus and was sent back to the town that had just asked Jesus to go. His mission field was the place that knew him at his worst.
gerasene-demoniac-luk.reflectionQuestion: Is there somewhere you would rather not go back to, that might be exactly where you are useful?
gerasene-demoniac-luk.distinctive: Luke alone puts him at Jesus' feet — the posture of a disciple sitting under a teacher — and alone says the townspeople were seized with great fear. Mark spends his detail on the chains and the self-harm beforehand; Matthew has two men and no history. Luke's interest is in what the man became: clothed, sane, and sitting down to learn.

bleeding-woman-luk.quote: But Jesus said, “Someone did touch me, for I perceived that power has gone out of me.”
details: Luke says she had spent all her living on physicians and could not be healed by any.
When Jesus asked who touched Him, everyone denied it.
She declared in front of all the people why she had touched Him.
bleeding-woman-luk.whatHappened: A woman who had bled for twelve years and spent everything she had on doctors came up behind Him and touched the edge of His cloak. The bleeding stopped at once. Jesus asked who had touched Him; everyone denied it. She came trembling and explained in front of the whole crowd why she had done it, and how she had been healed immediately.
bleeding-woman-luk.hopeMeaning: She had wanted to take the healing invisibly and go. Instead she had to say out loud, in public, what had been wrong and what she had done about it — and Luke records that as the moment she was called daughter.
bleeding-woman-luk.reflectionQuestion: What would it cost you to say out loud what you have been quietly carrying?
bleeding-woman-luk.distinctive: Luke, alone of the three, has everyone deny touching Him, and has Jesus insist — someone did touch me, for I perceived that power has gone out of me. He also has her declare her reason in the presence of all the people. Mark's version keeps the doctors who made her worse; Matthew removes the search entirely. Luke makes it a public examination.

jairus-daughter-luk.quote: But He put them all outside, and taking her by the hand, He called, saying, “Child, arise!”
details: Luke notes she was his only daughter, about twelve years old.
Luke adds that the mourners knew she was dead — the ridicule was informed.
Jesus told them to give her something to eat.
jairus-daughter-luk.whatHappened: Jairus' only daughter, about twelve, was dying. Word came that she had died and there was no point troubling the teacher, but Jesus told him only to believe. At the house He put the mourners out, took her hand and called her to get up. Her spirit returned, she rose immediately, and He told them to give her something to eat.
jairus-daughter-luk.hopeMeaning: Luke says the mourners knew she was dead — their laughter was not ignorance. And still the last instruction is domestic: feed her. The extraordinary ends in someone fetching a meal.
jairus-daughter-luk.reflectionQuestion: What ordinary care might be the right response to something you are treating as too big for that?
jairus-daughter-luk.distinctive: Luke alone says she was his only daughter, and alone adds that the mourners were ridiculing Him knowing that she was dead — closing off the reading that they were simply mistaken. Mark keeps the Aramaic words; Matthew removes the messengers entirely. Luke sharpens the fact that everyone in the room was certain.

feeding-5000-luk.quote: They ate and were all filled. They gathered up twelve baskets of broken pieces that were left over.
details: Luke has them seated in groups of about fifty.
The disciples' suggestion was to send everyone away to find their own food.
Five loaves, two fish, twelve baskets left.
feeding-5000-luk.whatHappened: As the day wore on the disciples suggested sending the crowd away to find food and lodging. Jesus told them to give the people something to eat themselves. Seated in groups of about fifty, five thousand men were fed from five loaves and two fish, and twelve baskets of scraps were collected.
feeding-5000-luk.hopeMeaning: The disciples' instinct was to disperse the problem — send them away, let them sort themselves out. They were told to feed them instead, with what they had, which was obviously not enough.
feeding-5000-luk.reflectionQuestion: Is there a need you have been hoping will resolve itself elsewhere?
feeding-5000-luk.distinctive: Luke keeps the orderly seating in groups of fifty and sets the whole scene just after the disciples return from being sent out on their own — so the men who have just been given authority are the ones who suggest sending the crowd away. Mark explains the motive as sheep without a shepherd; John names the boy; Matthew counts the women and children.

transfiguration-luk.quote: As He was praying, the appearance of His face was altered, and His clothing became white and dazzling.
details: In Luke it happens while He is praying — that is why they went up.
Moses and Elijah spoke about His departure, which He was to accomplish at Jerusalem.
The disciples were heavy with sleep and nearly missed it.
transfiguration-luk.whatHappened: Jesus took three disciples up the mountain to pray, and as He prayed His face changed and His clothes became dazzling. Moses and Elijah appeared and spoke about His coming departure at Jerusalem. The disciples were heavy with sleep; when they came fully awake they saw the glory. Peter offered to build shelters, not knowing what he was saying.
transfiguration-luk.hopeMeaning: It happened during prayer, and the men who came to pray nearly slept through it. Luke does not treat that as scandalous — just true. Being present and being alert are not the same thing, and the glory did not wait for them.
transfiguration-luk.reflectionQuestion: What might you be sleeping through because it came during something ordinary?
transfiguration-luk.distinctive: Luke alone gives the reason they went up — to pray — and alone says the change happened as He was praying. He alone reports what Moses and Elijah were discussing: His departure, to be accomplished at Jerusalem. And he alone admits the disciples were heavy with sleep. Matthew has them fall on their faces in terror; Mark has Peter babbling in fear.

boy-with-demon-luk.quote: But Jesus rebuked the unclean spirit, healed the boy, and gave him back to his father.
details: Luke says he was the man's only child.
The disciples had tried and failed.
Luke ends the sentence by handing the boy back to his father.
boy-with-demon-luk.whatHappened: A man begged Jesus to look at his only son, whom the disciples had been unable to help. As the boy came, he was thrown down and convulsed. Jesus rebuked the spirit, healed him, and gave him back to his father — and everyone was astonished at the majesty of God.
boy-with-demon-luk.hopeMeaning: Luke's sentence ends with the boy being handed back, the same phrase he used at Nain. Healing in Luke keeps finishing with someone being returned to the person who loves them.
boy-with-demon-luk.reflectionQuestion: Who would you most want handed back to you?
boy-with-demon-luk.distinctive: Luke alone says the boy was an only child — a detail he also gives the widow at Nain and Jairus' daughter — and alone ends with Jesus giving him back to his father. Mark's account is the long one, centred on the father's "help my unbelief"; Matthew's turns to the disciples and the mustard seed. Luke's is the shortest and closes on the handover.

crippled-woman-luk.quote: Ought not this woman, being a daughter of Abraham whom Satan had bound eighteen long years, be freed from this bondage on the Sabbath day?
details: She had been bent double for eighteen years and could not straighten up at all.
She did not ask — Jesus saw her and called her over.
The synagogue ruler complained to the crowd rather than to Jesus directly.
crippled-woman-luk.whatHappened: A woman bent double for eighteen years was in the synagogue. Jesus saw her, called her over, told her she was free of it, and laid hands on her — and she straightened up. The synagogue ruler objected to the crowd that there were six other days for healing. Jesus pointed out that they untie an ox on the Sabbath, and asked whether this daughter of Abraham should wait longer.
crippled-woman-luk.hopeMeaning: For eighteen years she could not look anyone in the face. The argument that follows is about whether her freedom could have waited one more day, and the answer is that it could not — the delay itself was the offence.
crippled-woman-luk.reflectionQuestion: Is there something you have told yourself can wait a little longer?

man-with-dropsy-luk.quote: Jesus, answering, spoke to the lawyers and Pharisees, saying, “Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath?”
details: Jesus was a dinner guest, and was being watched closely.
The man with dropsy was simply there, in front of Him.
He asked the question first, was met with silence, healed the man and let him go.
man-with-dropsy-luk.whatHappened: At a Sabbath meal in a leading Pharisee's house, where He was being watched, a man with dropsy was in front of Him. Jesus asked the lawyers and Pharisees outright whether it was lawful to heal on the Sabbath. They said nothing. He healed the man, let him go, and asked whether any of them would leave a son or an ox in a well until the next day.
man-with-dropsy-luk.hopeMeaning: He asked permission of a room that would not answer, and then acted anyway. The silence did not stop Him, and the man was quietly let go before the argument continued.
man-with-dropsy-luk.reflectionQuestion: What have you not done because you were waiting for someone to say it was allowed?

ten-lepers-luk.quote: Were there none found who returned to give glory to God, except this foreigner?
details: They stood at a distance, as the law required, and shouted.
They were cleansed as they went, not before they set off.
The one who came back was a Samaritan — a foreigner.
ten-lepers-luk.whatHappened: Ten men with leprosy stood at a distance and shouted for mercy. Jesus told them to go and show themselves to the priests, and they were cleansed on the way. One turned back, praising God loudly, and fell at Jesus' feet — and he was a Samaritan. Jesus asked where the other nine were.
ten-lepers-luk.hopeMeaning: All ten were healed, including the nine who did not come back. The gift was not withdrawn from the ungrateful. What the one who returned received on top of it was being told his faith had made him well.
ten-lepers-luk.reflectionQuestion: What have you received and never gone back to say anything about?

blind-at-jericho-luk.quote: Jesus said to him, “Receive your sight. Your faith has healed you.”
details: Luke places this as Jesus approaches Jericho rather than leaving it.
He asked what the noise was about before he started shouting.
Afterwards the whole crowd praised God, not just the man.
blind-at-jericho-luk.whatHappened: A blind man begging by the road heard a crowd going past and asked what was happening. Told that Jesus was passing, he began shouting for mercy, and kept shouting when told to be quiet. Jesus stopped, had him brought over, and asked what he wanted. He received his sight, followed, and glorified God — and all the people praised God too.
blind-at-jericho-luk.hopeMeaning: He had to ask what the commotion was before he could ask for anything at all. Luke notices that: the man had no way of knowing his moment had come unless somebody told him.
blind-at-jericho-luk.reflectionQuestion: Who tells you when something worth shouting about is going past?
blind-at-jericho-luk.distinctive: Luke sets it as Jesus draws near to Jericho, where Matthew and Mark have Him leaving it, and Luke alone has the man ask what the noise means before he calls out. Mark names him Bartimaeus and has the cloak thrown aside; Matthew has two men. Luke alone ends with the whole watching crowd praising God.

severed-ear-luk.quote: But Jesus answered, “Let me at least do this”—and He touched His ear and healed Him.
details: This happens during His arrest, moments before He is led away.
The ear belonged to a servant of the high priest — one of the arresting party.
Luke is the only writer who records the ear being healed.
severed-ear-luk.whatHappened: As Jesus was being arrested, one of His companions struck the high priest's servant and cut off his right ear. Jesus said to let it go that far and no further, touched the man's ear, and healed him — and was then led away.
severed-ear-luk.hopeMeaning: The last healing before the arrest is done for a man who had come to take Him away, undoing the damage caused by someone defending Him. It is a small, almost invisible act of repair in the middle of a disaster.
severed-ear-luk.reflectionQuestion: Is there damage done on your behalf that you would want to undo?

resurrection-luk.quote: He isn’t here, but is risen. Remember what He told you when He was still in Galilee,
details: Two men in dazzling clothes, where Mark has one young man and Matthew an angel.
The women were told to remember, not simply informed.
The apostles thought it was nonsense and did not believe them.
resurrection-luk.whatHappened: The women came at dawn with spices, found the stone rolled away and the body gone. Two men in dazzling clothes asked why they were looking for the living among the dead, and told them to remember what He had said in Galilee. They remembered, went and told the eleven — who thought it was nonsense and did not believe them.
resurrection-luk.hopeMeaning: They were not given new information; they were told to remember something they already had. And the people they told dismissed it as idle talk. Being right and being believed are separate matters, and Luke records the gap without softening it.
resurrection-luk.reflectionQuestion: What have you already been told that you have simply not remembered?
resurrection-luk.distinctive: Luke has two men in dazzling clothes, and alone has them tell the women to remember what Jesus had already said in Galilee — the news is a recollection, not an announcement. He alone records the apostles dismissing the report as nonsense. Matthew has the earthquake and the guards; Mark ends in silence and fear; John follows Mary weeping alone.
